title: India Just Merged Its Two Biggest Power Lenders Into a $130 Billion Giant. Here's What It Means.
excerpt: PFC and REC approved a merger on Sunday that creates India's largest non-banking financial company, with a loan book bigger than some of the country's banks.
body:
India just approved the biggest financial sector merger in its power industry's history. The boards of Power Finance Corporation (PFC) and REC Limited — the two state-owned behemoths that fund nearly every major electricity project in the country — voted on Sunday to merge into a single entity with a combined loan book exceeding ₹11 lakh crore ($130 billion).

The deal will make the merged company India's largest non-banking financial company by assets, bigger than some of the country's mid-tier banks. REC will be absorbed into PFC, with REC shareholders receiving 88 fully paid equity shares of PFC for every 100 shares of REC they hold.

## Why This Merger Matters

The consolidation was first signalled in the Union Budget for 2026-27, when Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced that major public sector NBFCs would be brought together to create larger institutions capable of financing India's energy and infrastructure ambitions at scale.

India is in the middle of a massive build-out. The country needs to nearly double its power generation capacity over the next decade to meet industrial demand, electrify its expanding rail network, power a rapidly growing fleet of data centres for the AI boom, and deliver on an ambitious renewable energy target of 500 GW by 2030. None of that happens without a lender big enough to underwrite it.

"The merger envisions creating a finance powerhouse," PFC said in its exchange filing. The combined entity will focus on "power sector reforms and accelerating green energy initiatives, leveraging improved financial and operational capacities."

## The Numbers Behind the Giant

The merged company's portfolio will carry roughly 40 percent exposure to power distribution, 29 percent to conventional generation, 14 percent to renewables, 8 percent to transmission, and the rest to infrastructure, logistics, and miscellaneous projects. State-owned borrowers account for about 80 percent of the book; the private sector, 20 percent.

The combined gross non-performing asset ratio stands at roughly 1.3 percent — remarkably low for a lender of this size — and the return on assets is around 3 percent on a trailing basis. The valuation was assessed by Ernst & Young Merchant Banking Services and RBSA Valuation Advisors, with a fairness opinion from Nuvama Wealth Management.

## What Still Needs to Happen

The merger is far from done. It requires approvals from shareholders and creditors of both companies, the Reserve Bank of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the National Company Law Tribunal, and several other regulatory and governmental bodies. PFC has stipulated that the merged entity must continue to qualify as a government company under the Companies Act, with the Government of India retaining majority voting rights.

One wrinkle: PFC currently owns 52.63 percent of REC, and the government holds about 56 percent of PFC. After the share swap, the government's direct stake in PFC could fall to around 42 percent — below the 51 percent threshold required for government-company status. How Delhi structures its post-merger holding will be closely watched.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs invested in India's infrastructure story — whether through direct equity holdings, mutual funds with exposure to PFC or REC, or infrastructure bonds — this merger reshapes the landscape. The combined entity's sheer scale could improve its credit rating and lower its cost of borrowing, potentially making Indian infrastructure bonds more attractive to overseas investors. REC has separately approved raising up to ₹1.40 lakh crore through bonds, a signal that the funding pipeline is about to open wider.

The power sector has been one of India's most bankable stories over the past five years, and this merger gives it a single financing anchor large enough to stand alongside any infrastructure lender in Asia.
